interactions.label: A student examines a histology slide showing an airway with no cartilage, no sub

params.question: A student examines a histology slide showing an airway with no cartilage, no submucosal glands, and no alveoli opening from its wall. Which structure is this most likely to be?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The trachea has C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings and seromucous glands in its submucosa. Their presence rules it out.
A bronchus retains irregular cartilage plates in its wall, distinguishing it from smaller airways.
Correct. A bronchiole has lost both cartilage and submucosal glands but has no alveoli opening from its wall — it is the last segment of the conducting airway.
A respiratory bronchiole also lacks cartilage and glands, but alveoli open from its wall — that defining feature marks the start of gas exchange.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the four features that change down the airway. A bronchiole lacks both cartilage and glands. What separates it from a respiratory bronchiole is the absence of alveoli in its wall.
Well done. Absent cartilage, absent glands, and absent alveoli together identify the bronchiole — the last purely conducting airway segment before the respiratory portion begins.

interactions.label: Posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia is more common on the left side. Which devel

params.question: Posterolateral diaphragmatic hernia is more common on the left side. Which developmental event explains this asymmetry?

answers.text: The left lung bud arises later than the right

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both lung buds arise from the same respiratory diverticulum. The left has two lobar bronchi versus three on the right, but this does not affect diaphragm closure.

answers.text: The left pleuroperitoneal membrane closes later than the right

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The left pleuroperitoneal membrane seals the pericardioperitoneal canal slightly later, leaving a longer window during which abdominal contents can herniate into the thorax.

answers.text: The left phrenic nerve develops after the right

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The phrenic nerves are carried by the pleuropericardial folds, not the pleuroperitoneal membranes. Their timing does not determine the closure of the diaphragmatic opening.

answers.text: The heart occupies the left thorax and delays muscular closure on that side

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The heart sits in the pericardial cavity, separated from the pleural cavities by the pleuropericardial folds. Its position does not delay pleuroperitoneal membrane fusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pleuroperitoneal membranes close the pericardioperitoneal canals from below. The left membrane closes slightly later than the right, creating a longer vulnerable window on the left side.
Correct. The later closure of the left pleuroperitoneal membrane is the classic explanation for the left-sided predominance of congenital diaphragmatic hernia.

interactions.label: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops much lower in the thorax than the right

params.question: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops much lower in the thorax than the right. Which pharyngeal arch artery derivative is responsible for keeping it in this position?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The third arch gives rise to the common carotid arteries but has no relationship with the recurrent laryngeal nerve pathway.

answers.text: Arch of the aorta (left fourth arch derivative)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The aortic arch derives from the left fourth arch artery. The recurrent laryngeal nerves originally hooked under the sixth arch arteries, not the fourth.

Correct. Each recurrent laryngeal nerve originally looped under its respective sixth arch artery. On the left, the distal sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, later becoming the ligamentum arteriosum, which anchors the nerve low.

The left subclavian arises from the seventh intersegmental artery, not from a pharyngeal arch. It is the right recurrent laryngeal that hooks under the right subclavian after the right sixth arch regresses.

overallFeedback.feedback: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves originally hooked under the sixth arch arteries. On the left, persistence of the ductus arteriosus (left sixth arch) keeps the nerve low in the thorax. On the right, the sixth arch regresses and the nerve migrates upward.
Correct. The left sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, keeping the left recurrent laryngeal nerve low. The right sixth arch regresses, allowing the right nerve to ascend to the subclavian.

interactions.label: An isolated ventricular septal defect causes cyanosis because deoxygenated blood

params.question: An isolated ventricular septal defect causes cyanosis because deoxygenated blood crosses from the right ventricle into the left ventricle.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: After birth, left ventricular pressure exceeds right. In an isolated VSD, the shunt is left to right — oxygenated blood recirculates through the lungs. Cyanosis requires deoxygenated blood to enter the systemic circulation, which only occurs when pulmonary outflow obstruction reverses the gradient, as in tetralogy of Fallot.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. After birth, left ventricular pressure exceeds right. Blood shunts left to right through a VSD, recirculating oxygenated blood through the lungs. This overloads the pulmonary circulation but does not cause cyanosis. Cyanosis requires a right-to-left shunt, as in tetralogy of Fallot.

interactions.label: On a posteroanterior chest radiograph, the right heart border is no longer visib

params.question: On a posteroanterior chest radiograph, the right heart border is no longer visible against the adjacent lung field. Using the silhouette sign, which part of the lung is most likely consolidated?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The right upper lobe lies above and lateral to the hilum. Its consolidation obliterates the superior mediastinal border, not the right heart border.
Correct. The right middle lobe lies directly against the right heart border (right atrium). When it consolidates, the tissue-density interface disappears and the border is lost.
The right lower lobe sits posteriorly and inferiorly. Its consolidation obscures the right hemidiaphragm, not the heart border.
The lingula lies against the left heart border. Its consolidation would obliterate the left heart border, not the right.

overallFeedback.feedback: The silhouette sign states that a border disappears when the adjacent lung loses its air. The right heart border lies directly against the right middle lobe — consolidation here replaces air with tissue density, erasing the border.
Correct. The silhouette sign localises pathology by identifying which border is lost. The right middle lobe abuts the right heart border; the lingula abuts the left.

interactions.label: At the midaxillary line, the lung border ends at the eighth rib while the pleura

params.question: At the midaxillary line, the lung border ends at the eighth rib while the pleural reflection continues to the tenth rib. What occupies the gap between these two borders during quiet breathing?

answers.text: The costodiaphragmatic recess — pleura is present but the lung does not extend here

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The costodiaphragmatic recess is a potential space lined by parietal pleura where the lung only enters during deep inspiration. Fluid collects here, and a needle can safely access the pleural space without injuring the lung.

answers.text: The costomediastinal recess — where the pleura reflects around the heart

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The costomediastinal recess is an anterior structure where left pleura reflects over the pericardium. It is not located at the midaxillary line.

answers.text: An air-filled space with no pleural lining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The pleura does extend to the tenth rib at this line. The space is lined by parietal pleura on both surfaces, making it a potential pleural space, not an unlined cavity.
The oblique fissure runs within the lung parenchyma, separating the upper and lower lobes. It does not account for the gap between the lung border and the pleural reflection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pleura always extends two ribs lower than the lung. At the midaxillary line, this creates the costodiaphragmatic recess between the eighth and tenth ribs — a space lined by pleura but not occupied by lung during quiet breathing.
Correct. The costodiaphragmatic recess is clinically important — it is where pleural effusion first collects and where thoracocentesis can be performed safely during quiet breathing.
